judge.reasoning:
This report is well-matched to the brief and would genuinely help the owner shortlist territory. 

Tool/metric selection (9): The agent picked exactly the metrics that matter for premium test prep — median household income, six-figure household share, college-or-above attainment, STEM degree share, median home value (as a wealth proxy), and crucially the teen (10-19) age band that is the literal customer. This intersection of "means + motivation + student pipeline" is precisely the right ICP framing. Nothing important is obviously missing except perhaps direct school-district-quality data, which the brief emphasizes ("top-ranked public school districts") and is only proxied via attainment.

Section relevance (9): All five sections map to the brief — top counties, wealth/willingness-to-pay, education culture/STEM, the student pipeline (Section 4 is especially strong and business-savvy, translating age shares into estimated teen headcounts), and metro-level go-to-market framing. No filler sections (no unemployment, race, commute-time padding). Slight ding because the brief's core criterion — school district rankings — is never directly addressed.

Narrative (8): Specific, data-anchored, and actionable. It names concrete counties, cites real numbers, distinguishes volume markets (Suffolk, Monmouth) from density/affluence markets (Nassau, Bergen), flags Western CT as a home-value outlier, and gives differentiated recommendations (emphasize admissions consulting in Trenton-Princeton, STEM-rigor marketing in high-STEM counties). Minor overreach: it treats attainment as a stand-in for "education-focused families" without acknowledging that district quality and existing competitor saturation aren't measured.

Data plausibility (8): Incomes ($140K–$184K for these counties), home values ($765K–$1.06M, Nassau seven figures), and ~63-67% college attainment are all in the right ballpark for these affluent tri-state counties. Teen-share figures (~12-15%) and derived headcounts are sensible. Some tension exists between county-level attainment (~63-67%) and the parent CBSA figure (NY-Newark 53.7%), which is internally consistent (metro dilutes affluent counties) but the very high STEM-degree shares (44-55% of adults) look somewhat inflated/ambiguously defined.

Visualization (7): Bubble charts are appropriate for the multi-dimensional income/education/population comparisons, and bars fit the income rankings. However there are recurring flaws: several bar charts are truncated to only 5 categories and Section 2/3 bars encode a second variable in the "percentage" field or split college vs. STEM into interleaved bars that a simple bar chart handles awkwardly (a grouped bar would be better). The heavy reliance on repeated bubble charts across sections is somewhat redundant. No distribution charts (violin/histogram) are used, which is acceptable since the data is aggregated point estimates rather than distributions.

Overall (8): Coherent, ICP-aligned, actionable, and presentation-ready with light polish. Held back from 9+ by the absence of direct school-district-quality data (a stated must-have), some redundancy in visuals, and slightly overstated STEM figures.
